The paper was published in the Journal of Applied Physics, Vol. 64, No. 8, on October 15, 1988.
The author, R.T. Ling, was affiliated with the Northrop Aircraft Division in Hawthorne, California.
The paper demonstrates that electromagnetic wave scattering and fluid flow phenomena are mathematically analogous boundary value problems.
The transformed Helmholtz equation for Debye amplitude functions is elliptic, making it a well-posed problem with unique and stable solutions.
The scattering problem involves a plane wave with wavelength λ and frequency ν propagating in the positive z-direction.
The incident electric field is polarized along the x-axis with amplitude Eⁱ = x e^(ikz).
The wave number k = 2π/λ is a fundamental parameter in the scattering analysis.
The intrinsic admittance of free space is Y = √(2/μ).
The example problem uses ka = 2.9, where a is the sphere radius.
The Debye amplitude functions exhibit large gradients in a 'strong interaction region' near the sphere surface, analogous to boundary layers in fluid flow.
Outside the strong interaction region is an asymptotic region where Debye amplitude functions vary slowly and approach far-field limiting values.
The optical theorem provides a relationship between total scattering cross section and forward scattering amplitude for energy conservation verification.
Surface current density is obtained from K = n × H = H_φ θ̂ - H_θ φ̂, where n is the outward normal vector.
The finite difference grid used in the example is 77 × 33 points.
Second-order accurate finite difference expressions are used for both boundary and interior points.
The cot θ(∂f/∂θ) term in the transformed Helmholtz equation requires special treatment at θ = 0 and θ = π.
The coordinate transformation θ → -θ shows that f(r,θ) = f(r,-θ) due to spherical symmetry.
The bistatic radar cross section σ₁(θ) and σ₂(θ) are computed from generalized scattering amplitudes S₁ and S₂.
The total radar cross section σᵣ is obtained by integrating bistatic cross sections over all scattering angles.
The paper notes that wave scattering problems are simpler than nonlinear fluid dynamic problems due to linearity.
Wave scattering problems avoid complications like shock discontinuities, boundary layers, turbulence, and vortex flows present in CFD.
The generalized scattering amplitude concept eliminates the oscillatory nature of field variables in infinite space.
The paper provides ready generalization to nonmetallic obstacles like dielectrics with appropriate modifications to surface boundary conditions.
The method can handle arbitrary orthogonal curvilinear coordinate systems, including numerically generated body-fitted grids.
A recent application mentioned is scattering by an airfoil-shaped perfect conductor using body-fitted curvilinear coordinates.
